name: What if the estimate is lower than the final construction cost?

mainEntity.name: Why do estimates often come in lower than the final bill, and how can I prevent that?
mainEntity.text: Why do estimates often come in lower than the final bill, and how can I prevent that?

acceptedAnswer.text: A lower-than-expected estimate usually happens because the original budget did not fully capture the real scope. Common causes include incomplete drawings, underestimated finish selections, missing permit or engineering costs, site surprises, and change orders requested after the job begins. In Los Angeles, these problems are more likely when a project involves an older home, hillside lot, or custom luxury finishes. The best way to reduce the gap between estimate and final cost is to insist on a detailed scope of work, realistic allowances, written exclusions, and a contingency budget. Owners should also verify whether the estimate includes supervision, cleanup, temporary protection, and utility upgrades. If those items are not listed, they may appear later as additional charges. A transparent estimate is not just about price; it is about making the final outcome predictable.
acceptedAnswer.description: Estimates run low when plans are incomplete, allowances are unrealistic, hidden site conditions appear, or scope changes after the bid. The best protection is a detailed scope, realistic allowances, a contingency reserve, and clear exclusions before work starts.
